case_name: State Bank of India & Ors. v. Manoj Kumar Das & Ors.
holding_summary: A three-judge Bench (CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana) declined to interfere with the NCLAT's 30 June 2026 order, which had affirmed NCLT Mumbai's direction that provident fund, gratuity and pension dues of former Jet Airways employees be paid in full and treated as falling outside the corporate debtor's liquidation estate. Lenders led by SBI had argued these dues should form part of the liquidation estate and be shared under the IBC waterfall unless a dedicated PF/gratuity fund existed at the commencement of liquidation. The Court found the lenders' points arguable but, given the peculiar facts of the case, declined to interfere, leaving the underlying legal questions open for a future case.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that employee provident fund, gratuity and pension dues can be treated as trust monies outside the liquidation waterfall even without a dedicated fund, which matters for resolution professionals, liquidators and secured lenders assessing recoveries in stressed-asset liquidations.

case_name: State of U.P. v. Jai Bir Singh
court: Supreme Court of India (Nine-Judge Constitution Bench)
holding_summary: A nine-judge Constitution Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant (with Justices B.V. Nagarathna, P.S. Narasimha, Dipankar Datta, Ujjal Bhuyan, Satish Chandra Sharma, Joymalya Bagchi, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M. Pancholi) revisited the 'triple test' for what constitutes an 'industry', laid down by the seven-judge bench in Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978). The Bench held that the 1978 triple test continues to govern industrial disputes still pending under the now-repealed Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, while refining aspects of that test, but held the 1978 ruling will no longer serve as the governing precedent ('sheet anchor') for disputes arising under the successor Industrial Relations Code.
why_it_matters: Ends decades of uncertainty over which establishments -- hospitals, educational bodies, government welfare departments, clubs -- qualify as an 'industry' for labour-dispute purposes, and narrows the expansive 1978 test's reach for future disputes; employers historically exposed under Bangalore Water Supply should reassess their position under the new Industrial Relations Code regime.

case_name: Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Union of India
holding_summary: The Supreme Court quashed a penalty for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax that had escalated from Rs. 12,000 in the original adjudication to Rs. 71,29,140 after the airline successfully appealed and secured a remand for de novo adjudication. Invoking the principle against 'reformatio in peius' -- that a litigant should not be placed in a worse position for having exercised a statutory right of appeal -- the Court held that mere delay in depositing tax already collected does not amount to 'failure to pay' attracting penalty under Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979, and directed refund of any penalty already paid, with 9% annual interest.
why_it_matters: Confirms that an appellate or remand process cannot be used to dramatically enhance a penalty beyond what was originally imposed, and clarifies that delayed remittance of tax already collected is legally distinct from non-payment -- relevant to any indirect-tax dispute where a taxpayer faces penalty escalation on remand.

case_name: Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that a financier's right of self-help repossession of a hypothecated vehicle cannot be exercised through force, deceit, or in breach of the loan agreement's terms, after Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company repossessed the appellant's commercial truck at 1 a.m. by breaking its steering lock without prior notice, following a loan default. The Court directed the financier to close the loan account, refund Rs. 4.5 lakh realised from the vehicle's sale with 6% annual interest, and pay Rs. 10 lakh compensation for mental agony and loss of livelihood, and separately directed RBI to ensure banks and NBFCs actually comply with its existing recovery and repossession guidelines, observing that those guidelines have 'existed only on paper'.
why_it_matters: Sharply raises the litigation and compensation exposure for banks and NBFCs (and their recovery agents) that repossess vehicles or other hypothecated assets without following RBI's fair-practice and due-process norms, and places RBI under a fresh judicial mandate to supervise actual compliance rather than merely issuing circulars.

case_name: National Highway Authority of India v. T. Younis & Anr.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that where a party files an application under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking correction, interpretation or an additional award, the three-month limitation period under Section 34(3) for challenging the award is reckoned from the date the arbitral tribunal disposes of that Section 33 application, regardless of whether the application is allowed or dismissed. The Court clarified that Section 34(3) does not distinguish between successful and unsuccessful Section 33 applications, but cautioned that where a Section 33 application is shown to be sham, frivolous or filed only to defeat limitation, courts may impose exemplary and punitive costs.
why_it_matters: Parties and counsel computing the limitation period for a Section 34 challenge after an unsuccessful Section 33 correction/clarification application now have clear Supreme Court authority that the clock still runs from the Section 33 disposal date, not the original award date, removing a recurring source of limitation disputes in arbitration challenges.

case_name: Union of India v. Sunil Biyani
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu held that no arrest can be effected under Section 69 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 for alleged tax evasion or fraud unless the order recording the officer's 'reasons to believe' for the arrest has first been communicated to the person concerned, including by electronic means such as registered email or the mobile number on record with the GST authorities. The Court also held that once a pre-arrest bail application is dismissed as not maintainable, a court cannot separately grant or extend interim protection from arrest, since that protection is ancillary to the pending application and cannot survive its dismissal.
why_it_matters: GST field formations must now communicate the Section 69 arrest order and its recorded reasons to the taxpayer before making an arrest, giving assessees a concrete procedural safeguard and a fresh window to seek anticipatory bail before any arrest is carried out.

case_name: Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC v. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta set aside the NCLAT's 2022 order and the CCI's 2021 order that had penalised Amazon Rs. 202 crore and purported to keep its already-approved 2019 investment in Future Coupons Private Limited 'in abeyance' over alleged suppression of facts in the merger notification. The Court held that once the CCI approves a combination under Section 31(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, it lacks statutory authority to keep that approval in abeyance or compel a fresh merger filing after the limitation period for review has expired. The CCI was directed to refund the penalty with 6% simple annual interest.
why_it_matters: Merging parties now have clearer assurance that a CCI approval of a combination is final and cannot later be suspended or reopened outside the Act's own review timelines merely on an allegation of incomplete disclosure, which matters for deal certainty in M&A and private equity transactions requiring CCI clearance.

case_name: Tata Steel Ltd. v. Varsha & Anr.
holding_summary: Arising from the Bhushan Steel Limited CIRP, the Supreme Court held that an operational creditor whose claim was admitted at a nominal quantified value of Re. 1 in an approved resolution plan cannot later revive the full, uncrystallised value of that claim through a pending civil suit or arbitration. The Court reaffirmed the 'clean slate' doctrine, holding that only claims crystallised and quantified as of the effective date of the resolution plan are payable on a pro-rata basis, and that claims not so crystallised stand abated, extinguished, waived or withdrawn once the plan is approved, dismissing both a pending civil recovery suit and connected arbitration references. The Court separately urged a legislative review of protections for MSME and other small operational creditors.
why_it_matters: Resolution applicants get further confirmation that the clean-slate principle protects them from stale, unquantified operational-creditor claims resurfacing years after a resolution plan takes effect, but operational creditors, especially MSMEs, are put on notice that they must ensure their claims are properly crystallised and quantified before the resolution plan is approved.

case_name: Rashmirekha Tripathy v. Sriram General Insurance Co. Ltd.
holding_summary: Laying down guidelines for assessing a deceased or injured claimant's income in motor accident compensation cases, the Supreme Court held that for salaried persons, the last available Income Tax Return ordinarily suffices to determine income, while for self-employed persons and business owners, tribunals should ordinarily take the average of up to three years' ITRs as the reference point for computing loss of dependency or loss of earning capacity.
why_it_matters: Motor Accident Claims Tribunals now have a clearer, standardised method for income assessment that reduces inconsistent approaches between salaried and self-employed claimants, narrowing the scope for disputes over quantum in future MACT claims.

case_name: Reliance General Insurance Company Limited v. Priyanka Das and Others
holding_summary: Deciding connected appeals arising from a single motorcycle-truck collision, the Supreme Court held, first, that the compensation multiplier for a deceased bachelor's death must be selected based on the deceased's own age under the standardised matrix in Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi, not the age of the deceased's parents, applying multiplier 16 for the deceased's age bracket of 31-35 years. Second, on the injured pillion rider's claim, the Court held that functional earning capacity cannot be discounted merely because the claimant continued in the same employment role after the accident, enhancing her compensation to over Rs. 3.77 crore after she was certified as suffering 100% permanent disability, holding that earning capacity in the open labour market, not continued retention in a specific job, is the correct test.
why_it_matters: Confirms two claimant-favourable principles for MACT litigation: the age of the deceased (not the dependants') governs the multiplier for a bachelor's death, and continued employment post-accident does not by itself defeat a claim of substantial or total loss of future earning capacity.

case_name: The New India Assurance Company Limited & Ors. v. M/S Louis Dreyfus Commodities India Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: Ruling on a marine cargo turnover-based insurance policy where a fire caused losses exceeding the insured's declared annual turnover coverage, the Supreme Court held that Section 64VB of the Insurance Act, 1938 places an absolute embargo on an insurer assuming additional risk unless the corresponding premium is received in advance. Since the insured paid additional premium to cover the enhanced turnover only after the fire loss had already occurred, the Court held the insurer was not liable beyond the originally covered sum insured, and that an insurance agent's assurance of extended cover cannot override the statutory requirement of advance premium payment.
why_it_matters: Businesses operating turnover-linked or declaration-based insurance policies must ensure additional premium for enhanced coverage is paid before any loss event, not after; an agent's informal assurance of extended cover will not bind the insurer if Section 64VB's advance-premium requirement was not actually satisfied.

case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sayona Colors Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R. Mahadevan set aside a consumer commission award in favour of an insured that had claimed Rs. 28.2 crore for a 2011 godown fire, holding on forensic findings that the fire was the result of deliberate arson rather than an accidental short circuit, and that the claim coincided suspiciously with a recent enhancement of insurance coverage. The Court held that once fraud in an insurance claim is established, no relief, even partial, can be granted to the claimant, and directed constitution of a Special Investigation Team to probe the fraudulent claim.
why_it_matters: Confirms that Indian courts will not apportion 'partial genuine loss' relief once fraud is established in an insurance claim, and signals that egregious fraudulent claims can trigger criminal investigation via a court-ordered SIT even though the dispute originated as a civil consumer complaint.

case_name: Dr. Bais Surgical and Medical Institute Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. v. Dhananjay Pande
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that an investor whose name was never entered in a company's register of members can nonetheless maintain a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, so long as the company's own conduct consistently recognised him as a stakeholder. On the facts, the respondent had invested substantial funds and was treated as Managing Director and 'co-owner', even though share certificates were never formally issued in his name; the Court held that formal non-entry in the statutory register could not defeat his substantive rights as a member.
why_it_matters: Companies cannot defeat a minority-oppression petition on the purely technical ground that the petitioner's name does not appear in the register of members where the company's own conduct, accepting investment, allotting a managerial role, treating the investor as a stakeholder, shows he was in substance a member; this closes off a common preliminary-objection strategy in oppression and mismanagement litigation.
